Maladaptive Strategies.value: I try hard to control my emotions
I distract myself with something else
I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied

Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: For a 64-year-old male politician whose trauma was as a relief worker in a war zone, this self-harm item is the only clearly incoherent element. The rest of the profile depicts classic war-related PTSD with sensory/social triggers, intrusive fragmented memories, and hypervigilant threat monitoring, plus avoidance/emotion-control strategies. In contrast, deliberate physical self-harm as a distraction is not supported by the surrounding pattern: there are no negative appraisal items suggesting self-punishment, shame, or self-directed hostility, and the formulation shows strong Triggers→Maladaptive Strategies links that are better matched by distraction and emotion-control than by self-injury. This item is not impossible, but within this profile it is the one element a clinician would most question as belonging to the same patient formulation.

vignette: Ahmed, a 64-year-old Middle Eastern man and former politician, has lived with the haunting memories of his time as a relief worker in a war zone for years. His experiences have profoundly impacted his daily life, leading him to seek psychological help after decades of coping through avoidance and distraction. The traumatic event that still haunts Ahmed occurred during a particularly volatile period when he was working in a war-torn city. One day, while distributing supplies, he witnessed a bombing that left the streets smoldering with the acrid smell of burnt rubber and metal. The explosion killed several civilians right before his eyes, including a young child who had been reaching out for help just moments earlier. The silence following the blast was deafening-a silence that felt even more terrifying than the cacophony of chaos. Since then, Ahmed has developed specific triggers that remind him of this horrific event. Interacting with strangers often brings back the sense of dread and vulnerability he felt in the war zone. He avoids talking to new people as much as possible, which has affected his ability to engage with constituents and colleagues in his political work. When military topics come up in conversation, Ahmed finds himself feeling overwhelmed and anxious, struggling to maintain composure. The olfactory cue-the smell of burnt materials-has been particularly difficult for him. Whenever he catches a whiff of something burning, it instantly transports him back to the scene of the bombing. This has led him to avoid areas with smoke or fire, even when there is no immediate danger. To cope with these intense feelings and memories, Ahmed employs several maladaptive strategies. He tries hard to control his emotions, often suppressing any signs of distress, which can lead to internal turmoil he struggles to express. When the memories start to overwhelm him, he distracts himself by throwing himself into work or other tasks. This overworking has taken a toll on both his health and personal relationships. Ahmed's belief that unusual silence indicates impending danger is deeply ingrained. He constantly scans his surroundings for signs of threat and repeatedly checks that doors and windows are locked. These behaviors have become habitual, causing him to miss out on social interactions and relaxation time with friends who no longer understand why he seems so anxious all the time. The memories themselves remain fragmented and terrifying. When he tries to recall the event, pieces of it come back in disconnected flashes-images of the explosion, the smell of burning debris, the sound of shattering glass-all of which bring back the same overwhelming terror he felt at the time. This makes everyday life feel like a series of small triggers waiting to set off intense emotional responses. Over time, these coping mechanisms have led to significant consequences. His work as a politician has suffered due to his avoidance behaviors and overworking habits. Colleagues have noticed that he is more distant and less engaged in discussions, which has affected the collaborative nature of political work. Personal relationships are strained as well; friends find it hard to understand why Ahmed avoids social gatherings or conversations that might touch on military topics. What finally brought Ahmed to seek help was a recent incident where the smell of burnt food in his home triggered a full-blown panic attack, leaving him unable to function for several hours. He realized he could no longer continue living this way, constantly on edge and unable to engage fully with life. Ahmed is most afraid that these memories will never truly leave him alone, haunting him forever. Yet, he also hopes that through therapy, he can find a way to manage his reactions and regain some semblance of normalcy in his daily life. He wants to be able to interact with people without fear, work effectively as a politician again, and enjoy the moments without being consumed by the past.
